title: Nanoscale imaging of ferromagnetic vortex dynamics with scanning NV magnetometry
authors: Jeffrey Rable, Jyotirmay Dwivedi, Nitin Samarth, Paul Stevenson, Arun Bansil, Swastik Kar
abstract: The generation and manipulation of spin waves at the nanoscale via magnetic vortices are of considerable importance because of their broad applications across magnonic and quantum technologies. Previously, fixed nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have been used to locally characterize vortex dynamics, and scanning NV magnetometry (SNVM) has been used to image vortices' static stray fields. Here, we demonstrate SNVM imaging of both the static and microwave fields generated by vortices in mesoscopic permalloy structures with $\sim$50 nm spatial resolution, achieving excellent agreement with micromagnetic simulations, while revealing the effects of disorder. We further demonstrate a 40$\times$ microwave field enhancement near a vortex core and image the disorder-dependent, spatially varying, evanescent decay of these microwaves. Our ambient, tabletop technique surpasses diffraction-limited techniques' resolutions by at least 5$\times$, with far greater accessibility and throughput than synchrotron radiation-based techniques, offering new opportunities in the study and development of magnonic devices.
summary: This work reports on using Scanning NV Magnetometry (SNVM) to image both static and microwave stray fields generated by magnetic vortices in permalloy films. The technique achieves high spatial resolution ($\sim 50 	ext{ nm}$) and successfully characterizes dynamic phenomena, such as field enhancements near the vortex core, validating its potential for developing nanoscale magnonic devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to image and characterize ferromagnetic vortex dynamics, including both static stray fields and microwave (MW) fields, at the nanoscale.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated high-resolution imaging of these dynamic magnetic fields in permalloy structures using SNVM, achieving field enhancements up to $40	imes$ near the vortex core.
method: Scanning Nitrogen-Vacancy Magnetometry (SNVM) is employed, utilizing Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) and Rabi oscillation measurements to map both DC and AC magnetic fields.
model_or_system: The experiments are performed on mesoscopic permalloy ($	ext{NiFe}$) thin films patterned into square or disc geometries. The analysis is heavily supported by comparison with micromagnetic simulations solving the LLG equation.
key_observables: Static stray fields (measured via ODMR frequency), microwave field amplitude (derived from ODMR FWHM and Rabi oscillations), and evanescent decay constants ($k$).
important_parameters: Spatial resolution ($\sim 50 	ext{ nm}$), MW field enhancement factors ($\sim 40	imes$), and characteristic decay lengths for different vortex modes.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes the power-broadened regime relationship between FWHM and $B_{	ext{MW}}$ holds, and that micromagnetic simulations accurately capture the underlying physics despite disorder effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate ODMR/Rabi maps comparing experimental measurements to simulation predictions for both square (wall mode) and disc (azimuthal mode) vortex structures, alongside analyses of field decay with distance.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by detailing the SNVM measurement techniques (static vs. dynamic fields), presenting results on patterned permalloy samples (square/disc), comparing these findings against detailed micromagnetic simulations, and analyzing specific physical phenomena like field enhancement and wave decay.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter magnetism, the use of NV centers to probe nanoscale magnetic dynamics is highly relevant to quantum sensing and open quantum systems characterization, providing a platform for studying spin-field interactions at unprecedented spatial resolution.
